articles.title: Prompt Injection Is the SQL Injection of AI Agents
articles.excerpt: You can't prompt your way out of prompt injection. Here's how I design AI agents for containment instead of hope. If you built web apps in the 2000s, you remember SQL injection. Someone typed '; DROP…
articles.body: You can't prompt your way out of prompt injection. Here's how I design AI agents for containment instead of hope. If you built web apps in the 2000s, you remember SQL injection. Someone typed '; DROP TABLE users; -- into a login form, and the database did exactly what it was told. Prompt injection is the same bug, wearing new clothes. An AI agent reads a web page, an email or a PDF, and somewhere in that text is a sentence written to look like an instruction. The model can't reliably tell your instructions apart from the attacker's, so sometimes it follows theirs. I'm Michael Petler, and I founded INASNAP . Our AI lab, INASNAP Labs, builds governed AI agents for businesses from startups through enterprise, and prompt injection is the risk I plan around more than any other.
articles.author: Michael Petler

articles.body: Freelancer Client Onboarding: A First-Week Checklist That Stops Scope Creep The first week with a new client decides how the whole project goes. Not the quality of your work — the quality of the setup. A project that starts with a clear kickoff, a written scope, and one agreed way to communicate rarely turns into a mess. A project that starts with "just send it over whenever" turns into scope creep, late replies, and an invoice nobody remembers agreeing to. Onboarding is not paperwork for its own sake. It is five small steps, done once, that stop the five most common freelance headaches before they start. 1.

articles.title: Batch Redaction Ownership for Property Invoices Using PDF Templates and Repository HTML
articles.excerpt: Batch throughput creates a dangerous incentive: approve the layout quickly and count every rendered property invoice as finished, even though the job is to remove personal data before sharing. Resolve…
articles.body: Batch throughput creates a dangerous incentive: approve the layout quickly and count every rendered property invoice as finished, even though the job is to remove personal data before sharing. Resolve that trade-off by giving one release owner authority over the redacted output, while the document owner approves presentation and engineering owns execution. TL;DR: choose a stored PDF template when a controlled page design is the constraint; choose HTML in the repository when layout changes should travel through code review. In both cases, bind approval to the exact layout revision and final artifact, and measure throughput at the sharing boundary. What page fired when the batch finished?

articles.body: TL;DR what: CVE-2026-119618 is a code execution flaw in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 module that affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach a server with HTTP/2 enabled can take full control of the server process, according to Red Hat. fix: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 fixes the flaw, Red Hat has shipped patched mod_http2 packages for RHEL 9 and 10, and Wiz advises restricting the Protocols directive to http/1.1 where no fix is available yet. who: Organizations that run Apache with h2 or h2c enabled, especially on Debian stable, Amazon Linux, Red Hat JBoss Core Services, Red Hat Hardened Images or standalone mod_h2 builds, where no fix has been published.

articles.body: The migration looked like an obvious win on economics. In one EvalShift run, the candidate model was: 58.8% cheaper 75.2% faster 0 failed or truncated calls Run economics. Same 16 calls on both sides, no failures, and every number a finance reviewer cares about moved the right way. Then the migration report returned: FAIL Not because the model crashed. Not because the API changed. Not because the output stopped parsing. It changed what the agent actually did. The verdict card. Five of seven budgets passed; the two that did not are the two that describe behavior. What failed I replayed 16 real examples against the source and candidate models. Across the run, 13.6% of evaluated comparisons regressed. The overall regression-rate budget actually passed.

articles.title: Why Does My Pod Take Exactly 30 Seconds to Die?
articles.excerpt: You run kubectl delete pod, and the pod sits in Terminating. You count. It disappears at almost exactly 30 seconds, every time. Thirty seconds is Kubernetes' default terminationGracePeriodSeconds. If…
articles.body: You run kubectl delete pod , and the pod sits in Terminating . You count. It disappears at almost exactly 30 seconds, every time. Thirty seconds is Kubernetes' default terminationGracePeriodSeconds . If your pod reliably takes the whole thing, it almost always means one thing: your app never received SIGTERM, or ignored it, and the kubelet had to SIGKILL it. SIGKILL means in-flight requests got cut off mid-response, open transactions were abandoned, and nothing got flushed. Every deploy, every node drain, every scale-down does this to you.

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P, then bounced twice and got lost. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

articles.body: Producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi explained why the development team behind the Ocarina of Time Remake toned down the ReDeads to make them less scary. If you grew up playing the original Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64, you were probably traumatized by some of the game’s famously frightening enemies like the Gibdos, ReDeads, and Dead Hands. These last two were particularly terrifying for young players at the time — partially because we were still kids, and partially due to the N64’s graphical limitations that forced our minds to fill in the visual gaps in the monsters’ designs. These enemies were a particular talking point when the Remake was first announced.
